paragraphs: Protein fitness optimization seeks sequence variants that work better for a particular application. The search is difficult because possible sequences are numerous, measured fitness information is sparse, and sequences consist of discrete choices. Together, these properties make it hard to identify a useful direction toward improved fitness.

VLGPO addresses this problem by representing protein sequences in a continuous latent space, where optimization can operate more smoothly. It combines a learned flow matching prior over mutations with a fitness predictor. The prior supplies a model of sequence variation, while the predictor guides the search toward variants expected to have higher fitness. The variational formulation connects these components through explicit prior and likelihood functions.

The authors report state-of-the-art results on two protein benchmarks with different levels of complexity. Those findings support the approach on the tested optimization problems. Its modular formulation also matters: separating the prior and fitness-related components creates a framework that can be customized for different protein design tasks.
icml-2025-a-variational-perspective-on-g.tldr: VLGPO combines a continuous protein representation, a learned mutation prior, and fitness guidance to optimize protein variants.

paragraphs: Orthogonal convolutional layers preserve norms, helping signals and gradients maintain stable magnitudes as they move through a network. This makes them useful in settings including adversarial robustness, generative modeling, and models with explicit constraints on sensitivity. Their practical use has been restricted by computational expense and limited architectural flexibility.

Adaptive Orthogonal Convolution, or AOC, extends an earlier construction called BCOP to address these restrictions. The paper targets obstacles involving common convolution features such as strides, dilation, groups, and transposed operations. Supporting these features matters because an orthogonal layer becomes more useful when it can fit the architectures practitioners want to build, rather than forcing those architectures into a narrow set of permitted operations.

The experiments show expressive models whose efficiency improves as they scale. The stated contribution therefore combines computational scalability with a wider range of feasible network designs. The authors also provide Orthogonium, an open-source Python implementation intended to make the construction available for further development and use.
icml-2025-an-adaptive-orthogonal-convolu.tldr: AOC makes orthogonal convolutions more scalable and flexible, enabling expressive architectures with improved efficiency at larger scales.

paragraphs: DiffMS tackles the task of generating molecular structures from mass spectra. Its aim is to propose structures directly from the measured evidence. The method also uses a known chemical formula, which provides a concrete constraint on the atoms available when constructing a candidate molecule.

A transformer encoder processes the spectrum using domain information, including formulas associated with peaks and neutral losses. A discrete graph diffusion decoder then generates molecular graphs while respecting the formula's heavy-atom composition. To strengthen the connection between internal representations and molecular structures, the authors pretrain the decoder on fingerprint–structure pairs. These are far more plentiful than paired molecular structures and spectra.

On established benchmarks, DiffMS outperforms existing approaches to generating molecules from spectra. Ablation experiments support the contributions of diffusion and pretraining, and performance consistently improves as the pretraining dataset grows in the reported experiments. The results show how abundant structural training pairs can help address the relative scarcity of spectrum-linked examples.
icml-2025-diffms-diffusion-generation-of.tldr: DiffMS combines spectrum encoding, formula-constrained graph diffusion, and extensive decoder pretraining to improve molecular structure generation.

paragraphs: Federated learning systems must balance useful models with protection for participating users. The abstract identifies a gap between two privacy settings: central differential privacy has benefited from the matrix mechanism, while distributed differential privacy offers stronger privacy protection but has lagged in model utility. DMM aims to bring these advantages together.

The main technical contribution is a cryptographic protocol that securely transfers sensitive values between client committees across training iterations. This transfer has constant communication overhead. It also accommodates changing participation and clients that drop out, both of which are practical concerns when training depends on many separate users rather than a permanently available group.

This protocol enables a distributed version of the matrix mechanism. Experiments show substantially improved model utility compared with earlier distributed differential privacy mechanisms, with little additional overhead. The significance is that the utility gains associated with the matrix mechanism can be made available in a distributed privacy setting while accounting for the participation patterns required by federated learning.
icml-2025-dmm-distributed-matrix-mechani.tldr: DMM brings matrix-mechanism utility gains to distributed private federated learning through efficient secret transfers between changing client committees.

paragraphs: ENSUR addresses confidence and fairness in recommender systems by producing prediction sets for users. Instead of treating recommendation quality solely as the accuracy of an individual prediction, it considers whether a set contains the ground-truth item, whether users across groups receive fair treatment, and how large the sets need to be.

The framework lets users specify a desired coverage probability, such as 90%. It provides guarantees for including ground-truth items, fairness across groups, and minimizing average prediction-set size. These objectives work together: a recommendation set should offer the requested confidence while remaining compact enough to be useful and satisfying the framework's fairness requirements.

The authors introduce GUFA to optimize this formulation efficiently. They derive upper bounds on risk and fairness quantities to accelerate optimization, alongside theoretical analysis of risk control, fairness control, and minimum set size. Experiments support the framework's effectiveness and agree with that analysis. The contribution is a unified statistical treatment of several recommendation goals that are often handled separately.
icml-2025-ensur-equitable-and-statistica.tldr: ENSUR generates compact recommendation sets with statistical guarantees for user-selected confidence and fairness across groups.

paragraphs: Prediction intervals can have acceptable coverage on average while behaving unevenly across batches of predictions. This paper studies that distinction for split conformal prediction. The false coverage proportion is the fraction of intervals that miss their targets in a particular inference set; its average can remain controlled even when individual realizations fluctuate substantially.

The authors observe that ordinary split conformal prediction may fail to control this proportion for a majority of repeated dataset splits. They propose CoJER, which controls false coverage proportion in probability. Its construction uses a characterization of conformal p-values in a transductive setting and includes an aggregation scheme designed to make the result more robust to modeling choices.

Real-data experiments show the intended proportion control for CoJER where standard split conformal prediction does not provide it. CoJER also produces shorter intervals than the compared state-of-the-art method for this stronger coverage objective, with intervals only slightly wider than ordinary split conformal prediction. This makes the distinction between average reliability and batch-level reliability practically consequential.
icml-2025-false-coverage-proportion-cont.tldr: CoJER controls the proportion of missed targets across prediction intervals in probability, with modest interval widening relative to standard split conformal prediction.

paragraphs: Building geometric symmetry into a neural network can reduce the parameters needed to represent relevant behavior, but it often increases computation. This paper focuses on horizontal reflection, called flopping, a symmetry relevant to many vision tasks. Its goal is to preserve that symmetry while keeping computation per parameter comparable to ordinary networks.

The key design choice is to represent features in two groups: those that stay the same under reflection and those that change sign. These correspond to the symmetry's irreducible representations. In this representation, the linear layers become block diagonal, which removes computations between the separate blocks and halves the required floating-point operations for those layers.

The approach reduces both operation counts and measured running time. That combination matters because a reduction in abstract arithmetic cost is more useful when it also translates into faster execution. The paper presents horizontal-reflection symmetry as a source of practical computational savings, supporting scalable networks that retain explicit control over how their features respond to mirroring.
icml-2025-flopping-for-flops-leveraging-.tldr: Separating mirror-symmetric and mirror-antisymmetric features enables symmetry-preserving networks with lower arithmetic cost and running time.

paragraphs: Forest-of-Thought addresses a weakness in language-model reasoning methods that follow a reasoning pass without adequately revisiting mistakes. Breaking a problem into steps or arranging possible steps into a tree can help, but an early flawed direction may still compromise the answer. The paper instead organizes reasoning across multiple trees.

These trees contribute to collective decision-making. Sparse activation selects the most relevant reasoning paths, helping concentrate computation where it is useful. A dynamic self-correction strategy allows errors to be addressed during reasoning, while consensus-guided decisions use agreement to help manage correctness and computational resources. Together, these mechanisms make path selection, correction, and coordination part of the reasoning procedure.

The experiments report significant improvements in reasoning capability when the framework is combined with these strategies, including greater precision and efficiency on complex tasks. The central implication is that additional inference-time computation can be organized around several interacting reasoning searches, with mechanisms for revising mistakes and choosing which paths deserve continued attention.
icml-2025-forest-of-thought-scaling-test.tldr: Forest-of-Thought coordinates multiple reasoning trees with selective activation, self-correction, and consensus to improve reasoning accuracy and efficiency.

paragraphs: Language-model watermarking aims to make generated text detectable as coming from a particular model. Existing approaches can introduce costs in generation speed, detection, text quality, or resistance to modification. GaussMark places the watermark in model weights, creating a structural signal without adding generation latency.

The method is based on Gaussian independence testing. It is motivated by observations that small additive changes to language-model weights can preserve, and sometimes improve, model quality. The paper develops formal statistical bounds for the watermarking procedure's validity and power, addressing both the reliability of its statistical conclusions and its ability to detect the embedded signal.

Experiments characterize GaussMark as efficient, reliable, and relatively resistant to corruption. They also show that it can be configured with essentially no loss of model quality. These findings support a practical route to watermarking through the model itself. The robustness claim remains qualified: the reported resistance to corruption is relative, rather than a claim that the watermark survives every possible alteration.
icml-2025-gaussmark-a-practical-approach.tldr: GaussMark embeds statistically testable watermarks in language-model weights without adding generation latency and with essentially no quality loss in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Circuit discovery tries to explain a language model's behavior by identifying the internal computational subgraph responsible for a task. The paper argues that many existing methods overlook how a circuit functions as a whole. They also require task-specific designs for corrupted activations, making the discovery process cumbersome and potentially inaccurate.

IBCircuit turns circuit discovery into an end-to-end optimization problem based on the Information Bottleneck principle. It seeks informative circuits holistically, addressing the collection of components as a connected explanation of behavior. The framework can be applied to a given task without manually designing corrupted activations for that task, reducing a source of specialized intervention work.

On Indirect Object Identification and Greater-Than tasks, IBCircuit finds circuits that are more faithful and minimal than those from recent related methods. The comparison covers both critical nodes and connections between them. These results support the usefulness of jointly searching for compact circuits that preserve task-relevant behavior, while locating the empirical evidence in the two evaluated tasks.
icml-2025-ibcircuit-towards-holistic-cir.tldr: IBCircuit uses Information Bottleneck optimization to find compact, faithful task circuits without task-specific corrupted activations.

paragraphs: Complex simulators can generate realistic synthetic observations even when the probability of a particular observation cannot be evaluated directly. Simulation-based inference addresses this difficulty, but Bayesian inference still requires a prior. This paper studies how to construct reference priors when the simulator's likelihood is unavailable.

Reference priors are designed to be minimally informative in a specific statistical sense. They maximize an expected Kullback–Leibler separation between prior and posterior, supporting inference without requiring strong subjective prior beliefs. The authors propose several likelihood-free learning methods that represent these priors through variational approximations and use different mutual information estimators to guide their construction.

Experiments show that the proposed methods can obtain good approximations to reference priors for simulation models. The contribution extends simulation-based inference to a prior-selection problem that has received comparatively little attention. The authors frame it as an initial step toward likelihood-free objective Bayesian procedures: the evidence supports the feasibility of learning these priors, rather than a completed solution for every complex simulator.
icml-2025-learning-likelihood-free-refer.tldr: The paper learns approximate reference priors for simulators using variational representations and mutual information estimation without evaluating likelihoods.

paragraphs: The paper studies nonlinear drift-diffusion equations on metric graphs, where physical processes evolve along connected edges. Such models describe phenomena ranging from transport inside biological cells to crowd movement. Conventional numerical methods can require substantial tailoring, particularly when the task involves choosing a model or identifying unknown parameters.

The proposed approach uses physics-informed DeepONets in a modular construction. It first learns three representative edge models for inflow, internal transport, and outflow. These learned models are then coupled through an edge-based domain decomposition method to solve the overall graph problem. This organizes the computation around the network's individual edges and their connections.

The authors illustrate accurate evaluation of coupled physical models and suitability for optimization and inverse problems on these networks. That matters because a useful solver may need to support both predicting behavior from known parameters and inferring parameters from desired or observed behavior. The contribution is a learned, physics-informed framework that connects these tasks within a graph-based representation.
icml-2025-physics-informed-deeponets-for.tldr: The method couples physics-informed DeepONets for different edge types to simulate drift-diffusion networks and support parameter identification.

paragraphs: Wireless communication and radar applications benefit from knowing how a channel varies within a particular environment. Generative modeling offers a way to learn this distribution, but existing approaches face difficulties with training-data quality, generalization, and physical interpretation. This paper incorporates channel physics into the generative model to address those issues.

The approach combines the physical compressibility of wireless channels with sparse Bayesian generative modeling. It learns a distribution over underlying physical channel parameters. The model's preference for sparse representations allows learning from compressed observations that an access point receives during its ordinary online operation, connecting the learning procedure to measurements already available in the system.

The resulting models are physically interpretable and can generalize across system configurations without retraining. This connects the representation being learned to properties of the channel, rather than tying it only to one configuration's measurements. The claimed generalization concerns changes in system configuration; the learning objective itself remains the channel distribution associated with an environment of interest.
icml-2025-physics-informed-generative-mo.tldr: Sparse Bayesian generative models learn interpretable wireless-channel distributions from ordinary compressed observations and transfer across system configurations without retraining.

paragraphs: Dataset distillation aims to replace a large training dataset with a small synthetic one while preserving model performance. DD3D adapts this idea to point clouds, whose orientations and numbers of points can vary. Those properties make techniques developed mainly for structured images harder to apply directly to three-dimensional data.

The paper theoretically establishes the importance of matching rotation-invariant features between real and synthetic examples. It introduces a point cloud rotator that aligns inputs to a canonical orientation, helping models learn these features. It also replaces direct optimization of fixed-size synthetic examples with a point-wise generator whose output resolution depends on how much noise is sampled.

This generator allows training with low-resolution point clouds and producing higher-resolution examples for evaluation. The authors report substantial memory savings and improved scalability from this arrangement. Experiments support DD3D on shape classification and part segmentation, including transfers across architectures and resolutions. The combined approach addresses both orientation consistency and the computational cost of representing detailed synthetic point clouds.
icml-2025-point-cloud-dataset-distillati.tldr: DD3D distills point-cloud datasets using orientation alignment and a variable-resolution generator to improve scalability and reduce memory use.

paragraphs: Certifying a classifier's resistance to adversarial changes can be computationally difficult. Sampling is more manageable, but sampling-based assessments alone do not provide the formal guarantees sought here. This paper develops a probabilistic relaxation of global robustness that aims to combine efficient evaluation with a precise guarantee.

The method samples an epsilon-net and applies a local robustness oracle to the sampled inputs. These local checks support a probably approximately global statement. A central theoretical result is that the required sample size does not depend on input dimensionality, the number of classes, or the learning algorithm. This is a claim about sample requirements, rather than a claim that every part of verification has identical cost across models.

The approach can therefore be applied to large neural networks beyond the reach of traditional formal verification. Experiments show better robustness characterization than the compared sampling methods and better scaling than formal methods. Its value lies in certifying the stated probabilistic relaxation, which makes a broader robustness guarantee computationally accessible.
icml-2025-probably-approximately-global-.tldr: Sampling combined with local robustness checks yields formal probabilistic global guarantees with sample requirements independent of input dimension and class count.

paragraphs: Machine-learning discussions often organize uncertainty into aleatoric and epistemic categories. This paper argues that this two-part vocabulary does not adequately express all the different quantities researchers want to discuss. As a result, statements about uncertainty can become inconsistent even when they use familiar terminology.

The authors offer a decision-theoretic perspective that relates formally defined uncertainty to predictive performance and statistical dispersion in data. The purpose is to distinguish concepts that may otherwise be grouped under the same label. This makes the intended meaning of an uncertainty quantity clearer by connecting it to the predictive and statistical questions being asked.

The paper also examines widely used information-theoretic quantities. It shows that these can estimate their commonly claimed targets poorly, while explaining why they may still help guide data acquisition. That distinction is central: a quantity's usefulness for selecting data does not by itself establish that it measures the particular uncertainty concept attached to it. The contribution is a more precise framework for interpreting such measures and their uses.
icml-2025-rethinking-aleatoric-and-epist.tldr: A decision-theoretic account clarifies uncertainty concepts and explains why useful data-acquisition measures can still poorly estimate their claimed targets.

paragraphs: Point-cloud augmentation should expose a model to varied shapes without disrupting the original object's underlying structure. This is difficult because point clouds are irregular and unordered. SinPoint addresses the tension between geometric variety and topological consistency by creating deformations designed to preserve topology.

The method uses a homeomorphism, a continuous and continuously reversible transformation, to preserve that structure. Sine functions generate smooth point displacements that simulate object deformation. A separate Markov chain augmentation process combines basic transformations through a random procedure, further broadening the distribution of training examples beyond the variation supplied by an individual deformation.

Across benchmark point-cloud datasets, the authors report consistent improvements over existing Mixup and deformation methods for shape classification and part segmentation. With PointNet++ and DGCNN, they report state-of-the-art classification accuracy of 90.2 on the real-world ScanObjectNN dataset. These results support augmentation that expands shape variation while explicitly preserving topology, with the randomized transformation process providing an additional way to enrich the training data.
icml-2025-rethinking-point-cloud-data-au.tldr: SinPoint improves point-cloud augmentation through smooth topology-preserving deformations and randomized combinations of basic transformations.

paragraphs: A language model's parameter count does not fully determine how quickly it runs. The authors find latency differences of up to 3.5 times among models of the same size. This motivates scaling laws that account for architecture and inference cost alongside the training resources normally used to predict performance.

The paper modifies Chinchilla scaling laws to jointly consider parameter count, training-token count, and model architecture. It also introduces a method for training inference-efficient models because similar training losses can still correspond to different downstream performance. The empirical study trains 63 models, spanning 80 million to one billion parameters and 1.6 billion to 30 billion training tokens, with varied shapes.

The resulting Morph-1B model improves inference latency by a factor of 1.8 while maintaining downstream accuracy relative to the compared open-source models. The experiments also show that wider, shallower designs can preserve accuracy while improving efficiency. These findings make model shape a practical part of choosing the accuracy–latency tradeoff, alongside size and training duration.
icml-2025-scaling-inference-efficient-la.tldr: Inference-aware scaling laws jointly optimize model size, training tokens, and architecture to improve language-model latency while preserving downstream accuracy.

paragraphs: Discrete diffusion and flow matching generate structures such as graphs through a sequence of denoising steps. The paper identifies dependencies between noisy distributions over time as a source of compounding errors: mistakes can accumulate and propagate as generation proceeds. It proposes a different construction intended to avoid that mechanism.

Simple Iterative Denoising removes dependence on previous intermediate states in the noising process. This changes how the intermediate noisy examples are related while retaining an iterative denoising framework. The authors further add a Critic that evaluates elements during generation according to their likelihood under the data distribution, selectively keeping some elements and corrupting others.

These two changes address complementary parts of generation: the noising construction removes the identified dependency, and the Critic directs which elements receive further revision. Empirical evaluations show substantial improvements over existing discrete diffusion baselines on graph generation tasks. The findings support reconsidering how intermediate states are constructed and how selective revision is controlled when designing generators for discrete structures.
icml-2025-simple-and-critical-iterative-.tldr: Simple Iterative Denoising changes noisy-state dependencies and adds selective Critic-guided revision to improve graph generation.

paragraphs: Probabilistic verification asks what can be formally established about a neural network's outputs when its inputs follow a probability distribution. This supports questions such as quantifying safety or checking demographic parity. The objective is to bound probabilities of output events, connecting network behavior to how inputs are distributed.

The proposed algorithm computes lower and upper probability bounds and refines them iteratively. It adapts bound propagation and branch-and-bound techniques from verification methods that do not explicitly reason about probabilities. The progressively tightened bounds provide a way to solve probabilistic verification problems using tools already effective for constraining neural-network outputs.

On several published benchmarks, the method reduces solving times from tens of minutes to tens of seconds. It also compares favorably with specialized algorithms for restricted versions of the problem. The theoretical analysis proves soundness and establishes completeness under mildly restrictive conditions with suitable heuristics. The distinction matters: reliable bounds are proved, while the completeness result depends on the stated conditions and heuristic choices.
icml-2025-solving-probabilistic-verifica.tldr: Branch and bound with bound propagation accelerates formal probability checks for neural networks while providing soundness and conditional completeness guarantees.

paragraphs: Models can learn associations involving features that correlate with labels in training data without supplying the intended predictive information. This paper analyzes that behavior in high-dimensional regression with a predictive core feature and a spurious feature. It quantifies learned spurious correlation using the data covariance and the strength of ridge regularization.

The analysis gives mathematical roles to feature simplicity and dependence. It represents the spurious feature's simplicity through its covariance spectrum and its relationship with the core feature through a Schur complement of the full covariance. It then proves a tradeoff: the regularization value minimizing in-distribution test loss lies in an interval where learned spurious correlation increases.

The paper also studies over-parameterization through a random features model, showing an equivalence to regularized linear regression. Numerical experiments on Gaussian data, Color-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 support the theory. Within this setting, optimizing ordinary test performance can therefore favor regularization choices associated with greater reliance on spurious information, connecting an accuracy objective to an explicit statistical account of shortcut learning.
icml-2025-spurious-correlations-in-high-.tldr: The paper quantifies spurious feature reliance in high-dimensional regression and proves a tradeoff involving ridge regularization and in-distribution test loss.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks process discrete events over time and offer a promising route to more energy-efficient neural computation. Converting an artificial neural network into a spiking one is a practical way to obtain competitive performance, but the resulting temporal behavior creates challenges that do not arise in the same form in the original network.

The authors identify temporal misalignment through a revealing observation: randomly rearranging spikes across layers can improve the converted network's performance. This indicates that the arrangement of spikes in time matters for conversion quality. Motivated by that observation, they introduce biologically plausible two-phase probabilistic spiking neurons to improve the conversion process.

The paper supports the proposed method with both theoretical analysis and experiments across several architectures. Evaluations on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, CIFAR10-DVS, and ImageNet achieve reported state-of-the-art results. The contribution links a specific temporal phenomenon to a neuron design that improves converted networks, advancing the practical use of spiking models through changes to their signal dynamics.
icml-2025-temporal-misalignment-in-ann-s.tldr: The paper identifies temporal misalignment in converted spiking networks and introduces probabilistic neurons that improve conversion performance.

paragraphs: Atomistic machine-learning models estimate energies and the forces that move atoms. Computing forces as derivatives of a potential energy enforces energy conservation. Direct force prediction can offer computational savings, but it removes that built-in guarantee, raising the question of whether training can adequately recover the missing physical constraint.

The paper investigates direct, non-conservative force models in microscopic simulations. It demonstrates problems including ill-defined convergence during geometry optimization and instability in several forms of molecular dynamics. The authors find that energy conservation is difficult to learn, monitor, and correct, unlike the comparison they draw with rotational symmetry. Prediction accuracy and speed therefore need to be considered alongside the behavior of the resulting simulation.

The authors suggest that combining direct force prediction with a conservative model might offer the best use of the acceleration. Such a combination could reduce the extra backpropagation cost while avoiding the pathological behavior associated with non-conservative forces. This is presented as a possible practical direction, rather than an established universally optimal solution.
icml-2025-the-dark-side-of-the-forces-as.tldr: Direct force prediction can cause problematic atomistic simulations, motivating possible combinations with energy-conserving models.

paragraphs: The paper investigates why state-space language models struggle with retrieving context despite their sequence-processing efficiency. It identifies a shared Gather-and-Aggregate mechanism in Transformers and state-space models: one head gathers relevant contextual information, and another integrates it into the representation. This work concentrates in a small number of heads.

That concentration creates bottlenecks. In a pruned Llama-3.1-8B, disabling one Gather or Aggregate Head reduces MMLU accuracy from 66% to 25%. The authors also show that successful retrieval can obscure a benchmark's knowledge demands: the pruned model succeeds on MMLU with these heads functioning while failing other knowledge benchmarks. Related bottlenecks appear in mathematics, broader reasoning, and dialogue tasks.

For state-space models, the retrieval difficulty appears as smoother attention patterns where effective gathering and aggregation require sharp transitions. Hybrid models assign aggregation to attention layers, and replacing a single relevant head in a pretrained state-space model with an attention variant improves retrieval and benchmark scores. These findings locate a consequential architectural difference in a few specific components.
icml-2025-understanding-the-skill-gap-in.tldr: A few Gather-and-Aggregate heads explain important retrieval bottlenecks and offer targeted ways to improve state-space language models.

paragraphs: Interacting particle systems describe collective behavior in settings such as biological networks, opinion formation, and robotic swarms. Because the particles are indistinguishable, reordering them should reorder their dynamics consistently. This paper investigates Transformers as approximators for these systems and for the mean-field descriptions that capture their collective evolution.

Experiments demonstrate approximation of several models, including Cucker–Smale flocking and milling and a mean-field system describing two-layer neural-network training. The theoretical analysis then connects finite-particle approximation to the infinite-dimensional mean-field vector field. Its premise is that a finite-dimensional Transformer effectively approximates the particle system's finite-dimensional vector field.

Under that premise, the authors bound the maximum discrepancy between an expected Transformer and the mean-field vector field by a function of the number of particles observed during training. They then obtain bounds on the difference between true dynamics and Transformer-generated dynamics. The result supplies a conditional mathematical bridge from learning finite interacting systems to approximating their collective evolution.
icml-2025-universal-approximation-of-mea.tldr: Experiments and conditional approximation bounds connect Transformers trained on finite particle systems to their mean-field dynamics.
